design_detail: Literature review (published as a Review Article) by three laboratory-medicine authors (University of California San Diego Center for Advanced Laboratory Medicine; Samsung Medical Center, Seoul) of reports of false-positive results on urine drug-screen immunoassays. The authors searched SciFinder (MEDLINE and CAPLUS) with the string 'false positive [drug] urine' for five predefined drug classes (amphetamines, tricyclic antidepressants, benzodiazepines, cannabinoids, opiates) and a miscellaneous class, and for a panel of over 60 common over-the-counter and prescription medicines, metabolites and illicit drugs; English, published after 2000; 173 articles, of which 62 held data on false-positive urine immunoassay results; older articles were used to clarify. Six tables give, for each report, the cross-reacting drug, assay platform and cutoff, immunoassay, concentration at which the false positive occurred, level of evidence (case report, retrospective chart review, spiking of standards into drug-free urine, therapeutic dosing) and reference. False negatives were excluded. No duplicate screening, flow diagram, appraisal tool or synthesis; filed as a narrative review with the editors' checklist, as the round brief directs. Read as the Advance Access version, whose pages (1-10) differ from the version of record; concentrations were read on the rendered pages because the text layer drops the micro sign.
can_establish: Which medicines and other substances had been documented, in reports published from 2000 to about 2014, to cause false-positive results on named urine immunoassays for amphetamines, MDMA, tricyclic antidepressants, benzodiazepines, cannabinoids, opiates, buprenorphine, methadone, PCP, LSD and barbiturates, with the concentration at which interference occurred where it was tested and the type of evidence behind each report.
cannot_establish: How often a given medicine makes a person screen positive in routine testing (frequencies exist for only a few reports), whether an interference applies to other or later assays (most were specific to one assay), or how many false positives have no known cause (the authors say most, without data); false negatives are not covered.

sample.inclusion_exclusion: SciFinder (MEDLINE and CAPLUS); string 'false positive [drug] urine'; English; articles published after 2000; included if they held data on false-positive urine immunoassay results; articles before 2000 used only to clarify current cross-reactivity issues (PDF p. 1, Materials and methods, 1st paragraph). Search dates are not stated beyond 'to present' (abstract).
sample.attrition: 111 of the 173 retrieved articles were set aside as holding no data on false positives (editors' arithmetic); they are not listed.
sample.selection_effects: A search built on the words 'false positive' finds reports of interference rather than reports of assays that did not cross-react, so the tables lean toward documented interferences; single case reports, chart reviews and spiking studies dominate; one search platform and English only.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable. In the cited reports: patients' prescribed or overdose medicines (case reports, chart reviews), dosing of volunteers, or pure standards or dissolved tablets added to drug-free urine or water.
exposure.polysubstance: Addressed only in one cited chart review (bupropion), whose investigators are said to have ruled out use of other drugs statistically (PDF p. 2).

comparison.controls: Not applicable; in the cited reports the reference is confirmation by GC-MS, LC-MS/MS or LC-PDA, or another immunoassay.

outcomes.instruments: Urine immunoassays named by manufacturer and platform in the cited reports (for example Syva EMIT II and EMIT II Plus, Roche KIMS, Microgenics CEDIA and DRI, Biosite Triage, Abbott AxSYM and TDx, Beckman Synchron, Siemens ADVIA, Bio-Rad TOX/See, and lateral-flow point-of-care cards and strips), with confirmation by GC-MS, LC-MS/MS or LC-PDA.
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors rank evidence (PDF pp. 1-2): weakest, exposure to the proposed interferent stated or two-dimensional structures compared; stronger, pure standard added at several concentrations to drug-free urine and the immunoassay tested; weaker variants use crushed tablets or water; chart reviews and quantitation in patients' specimens support but do not replace direct testing; dosing studies with confirmation of positives also count.
outcomes.operationalization: False positive: a positive immunoassay screen without the target drug, shown by negative confirmation, by spiking a candidate substance into drug-free urine, or, more weakly, by exposure to the candidate alone.

analysis.effect_sizes: As cited: concentrations at which false positives occurred and a few frequencies (see key findings); no pooling.
analysis.selective_reporting: False negatives excluded by design (stated, PDF p. 1); how often each interference occurs in routine testing is given only for a few chart reviews; the tables do not mark which entries rest on reports from before 2000 or on assays no longer in use.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Assay-specific reports of interference, most of them single case reports, chart reviews or spiking experiments; several interferents affected one assay and not others (efavirenz on 1 of 4 cannabinoid devices tested in one study; promethazine and chlorpromazine on 2 of 4 amphetamine assays; quetiapine on two of three tricyclic assays at therapeutic levels).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract calls the review inclusive and the introduction comprehensive (PDF p. 1), although the search used one platform, one string per drug, English and articles after 2000; the introduction states that in most cases the cause of a false-positive screen is unknown (PDF p. 1) without data. The conclusion that immunoassay positives should be treated as presumptive until confirmed by an independent chemical technique (PDF pp. 1, 8) follows from the evidence presented.

timeline.event: Earlier review of false-positive and false-negative results in clinical urine drug testing (Reisfield, Goldberger & Bertholf, 2009), cited as a previous review of the topic (PDF p. 1); not read.
Earlier review of commonly prescribed medicines and potential false-positive urine drug screens (Brahm et al., 2010), cited as a previous review (PDF p. 1); not read.

Clinical review listing agents reported to give positive (true or false) or negative results on each immunoassay; it draws on several of the same reports (efavirenz, sertraline, baby wash, PCP screens, MDPV) and disagrees on whether efavirenz affects the Drug Screen Multi 5 benzodiazepine test (PDF p. 12)

replication.where_it_stands: Each interference listed rests on case reports, chart reviews or spiking studies with specific assays; no systematic estimate of how often each occurs in routine testing was read for this card. The general conclusion, that screens are presumptive until confirmed, is shared by the 2017 clinical review.

funding.funder: Waters Corporation, which funded the UCSD clinical chemistry fellowship program (Acknowledgments, PDF p. 8).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the Advance Access PDF read.
funding.affiliations_note: Laboratory-medicine authors (UCSD Center for Advanced Laboratory Medicine; Samsung Medical Center, Seoul); the acknowledgment does not describe any role of the funder in the review. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A systematic review with duplicate screening and a stated appraisal of each report, updated for current assays, together with large laboratory datasets linking every unconfirmed positive screen to the person's medicines, giving how often each medicine produces a false positive on each assay.

domains.note: Platform, search string, language, years and counts (173 to 62) are stated, with one inclusion criterion; but one string per drug on one platform, no duplicate screening, excluded articles not listed, and older articles added without criteria.
Each entry carries its type of evidence and some limitations are named (no spiking for bupropion and sertraline); no appraisal within each type.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: None of the cited studies is by the authors; a colleague thanked in the acknowledgments is a co-author of one cited case study (Ly et al., 2012).
Mechanisms are labelled as hypotheses; one statement without data (most false positives have no known cause).

domains.domain: Balance of reports of interference against evidence of no interference
domains.note: The search string selects reports of false positives; where studies tested several assays, negative results are reported (for example three of four devices negative for efavirenz), but false negatives are excluded and the frequency of interference is rarely available.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard risk-of-bias instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3). Among narrative reviews this one is unusually explicit about its search and labels the evidence behind each entry, but its search is narrow, its selection unduplicated, and its subject (reported false positives) leans toward interferences that were found. It may be cited for which substances have been reported to cause false-positive results on which named immunoassays, at what concentrations and on what kind of evidence, for the few frequencies it reports (bupropion, sertraline, efavirenz, niflumic acid, ofloxacin), and for the conclusion that screening results are presumptive until confirmed by GC-MS or LC-MS/MS. It may not be cited for how often a medicine causes a false positive in general, for assays it does not name, or for false negatives; claims resting on it alone say their figures are second-hand.

key_findings.finding: Search and yield: SciFinder (MEDLINE and CAPLUS), string 'false positive [drug] urine' for amphetamines, tricyclic antidepressants, benzodiazepines, cannabinoids and opiates, a miscellaneous class and a panel of over 60 common medicines and illicit drugs; English, published after 2000; 173 articles, 62 of them with data on false-positive urine immunoassay results.

The authors conclude that immunoassay results should be treated as presumptive until confirmed by an independent chemical technique such as GC-MS or LC-MS/MS; they note that mass-spectrometry testing is limited or absent in many hospital laboratories, that confirmation results usually take several days, and that care decisions are therefore often made on presumptive positive screens.

False positives can come from structurally unrelated compounds and from metabolites, because antibodies bind three-dimensional structures; adding only the parent drug to drug-free urine without a positive result does not rule a medicine out.

Amphetamine screens and DMAA (an energy supplement): false positives on Roche KIMS and Syva EMIT II; added to drug-free urine, DMAA at 3.1 µg/mL triggered EMIT II and at 7.5 µg/mL KIMS; in urine of people taking DMAA, 6.9 µg/mL or more gave false positives on both.

Amphetamine screens and bupropion: in a retrospective chart review of amphetamine screens (Syva EMIT II Plus) not confirmed by GC-MS, 41% of the samples (53 patients) came from people taking bupropion; no spiking experiment showed that bupropion or its metabolites caused the reaction.
key_findings.note: The denominator is not printed; about 129 unconfirmed positive screens if 53 patients are 41% (editors' arithmetic). The share of people taking bupropion who screen positive is not given.

key_findings.finding: Amphetamine screens and other medicines: labetalol (three women prescribed it; GC-MS negative; a labetalol metabolite cross-reacts with several amphetamine immunoassays), metformin (case report, Biosite Triage), and promethazine (3 specimens) and chlorpromazine (6) on the Syva EMIT-MAM assay, all negative by LC-PDA; retested, all 9 were negative on Syva EMIT-A and Biosite Triage, but 2 were positive on the Agilent TesTcard 9.

Trazodone, through its metabolite m-CPP, gave false positives on the EMIT II Plus Ecstasy (MDMA) assay at 3.0 µg/mL but not on the EMIT II Plus amphetamine kit; on the Roche Amphetamines II assay m-CPP at 6.7 µg/mL or more gave positives while trazodone itself would need over 200 µg/mL; three patients with trazodone above 1.0 µg/mL and serum m-CPP above 0.85 µg/mL screened positive for amphetamines and were negative by GC-MS.

In 6 healthy men given two doses of the antibiotic ofloxacin 12 hours apart (study condition), no urine sample was positive before and all 6 were positive afterwards on the Abbott TDxFLx amphetamine/methamphetamine II assay, the lowest at almost four times the 300 ng/mL cutoff.

Tricyclic antidepressant screens: quetiapine was the only recently reported cause (carbamazepine and cyclobenzaprine were reported up to 2000); added to urine or water it triggered the Microgenics assay at 7.0 and 10.0 µg/mL, the Syva RapidTest at 100.0 µg/mL and the Biosite Triage above 1,000 µg/mL; in a patient who took a therapeutic dose 4 hours before (urine quetiapine 0.2 µg/mL), the Microgenics and Syva assays were positive and the Triage was not, which the authors attribute to metabolites.
key_findings.locator: Tricyclic antidepressants, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table II (p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Benzodiazepine screens and efavirenz (an HIV medicine): in a blinded study, the Biosite Triage 8 benzodiazepine test was positive in 46 of 50 patients taking efavirenz, while 47 of 50 not taking it were negative; two other point-of-care tests (Drug Control 008, Drug Screen Multi 5) and LC-MS/MS were negative on all the presumptive positives; spiking showed efavirenz and its metabolite 8-OH efavirenz caused the reaction.
key_findings.note: Moeller et al. (2017, PDF p. 12) say efavirenz interference occurs with the Triage 8 and Drug Screen Multi 5 tests, citing this study and another (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Benzodiazepine screens and sertraline: in a chart review of all specimens positive on the Abbott Architect and Aeroset platforms but negative on confirmation (January 2007 to December 2008), 26.5% (26 samples) of the false positives were linked to sertraline use; no spiking experiments were done.
key_findings.note: About 98 false positives in all if 26 samples are 26.5% (editors' arithmetic); the share of people taking sertraline who screened falsely positive is not given.

key_findings.finding: Cannabis (THC) screens and efavirenz: its glucuronide metabolite, not efavirenz or 8-OH efavirenz, gave false positives on three immunoassays (Microgenics CEDIA DAU Multi-Level THC, Biosite Triage TOX Drug Screen, Immunalysis Direct ELISA; cutoff 50 µg/L); in another study, Rapid Response test strips were positive in 28 of 30 patients taking efavirenz for at least 2 weeks, while the other point-of-care device (THC One Step Marijuana) and two automated immunoassays (Roche Cannabinoids II, Beckman SYNCHRON THC2) were negative.

Cannabis screens and niflumic acid (an anti-inflammatory medicine): all 55 urine samples from 5 volunteers taking it were positive for THC on Roche KIMS and negative on Syva EMIT; added to drug-free urine, about 2.5 µg/mL gave a KIMS response equal to the 50 ng/mL cutoff.

Cannabis screens and other causes: four commercial baby soaps gave positive results on the Vitros THC immunoassay at a 20 ng/mL cutoff (mechanism unclear); ibuprofen and naproxen gave false positives on the Syva EMIT d.a.u. cannabinoid assay (cutoff 20 µg/L) and on the Abbott TDx barbiturate assay in case reports.
key_findings.locator: Cannabinoids, 4th paragraph; Table IV; Table VI (p. 7)

key_findings.finding: Opiate screens and naloxone: naloxone at 6.1 µg/mL or more made urine 'opiate positive' on the CEDIA opiate assay (300 ng/mL cutoff), which the authors flag because most people treated for suspected opiate overdose receive naloxone.

Buprenorphine screens: the CEDIA buprenorphine assay (5 ng/mL cutoff) reacted to morphine, methadone, codeine, dihydrocodeine and morphine-3-glucuronide added to drug-free urine (printed as 0.12, 0.32, 0.03, 0.06 and 0.52 mg/mL), so heroin use, which can put large amounts of morphine in urine, could give a false-positive buprenorphine screen; tramadol also cross-reacted at the 5 ng/mL cutoff, and raising it to 20 ng/mL removed all tramadol false positives; amisulpride and sulpiride cross-react weakly but reach high urine concentrations.

Opiate and methadone screens and other medicines: quinolone antibiotics (levofloxacin, ofloxacin, pefloxacin, enoxacin, gatifloxacin, lomefloxacin, moxifloxacin, ciprofloxacin, norfloxacin) triggered four morphine immunoassays (300 ng/mL cutoff) when added to drug-free urine at 60-1,700 µg/mL depending on drug and assay, and ofloxacin did so in case reports; rifampicin triggered Roche KIMS opiates at 156-5,000 µg/L; pentazocine triggered the CEDIA heroin-metabolite (6-acetylmorphine) assay in a case report; methadone screens reacted to quetiapine (case reports), verapamil, diphenhydramine, tapentadol (6,500 ng/mL), several phenothiazines and clomipramine.

PCP screens: because PCP use is rare and PCP immunoassays are not specific, the authors say a positive PCP screen has a very low positive predictive value. Venlafaxine: after an overdose (serum venlafaxine above 24 µg/mL) an Abbott AxSYM PCP screen was positive and GC-MS negative, and spiked urine stayed positive even after fourfold dilution; in three other patients taking venlafaxine, the Syva RapidTest was positive at 25 ng/mL while three other PCP assays and GC-MS were negative.
key_findings.locator: Miscellaneous drugs, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table VI (p. 7)

key_findings.finding: PCP screens and tramadol: false positives with negative GC-MS in two patients who had taken tramadol in overdose amounts (DRI PCP assay on Siemens ADVIA 1800), with tramadol and N-desmethyltramadol each triggering the assay at 500 µg/mL in spiked urine (25 ng/mL cutoff), and in two further overdose patients on Syva EMIT II Plus.

PCP screens and MDPV ('bath salts'): after a patient with an apparent overdose who later died (post-mortem blood MDPV 1.0 µg/mL, no PCP), MDPV above 3.1 µg/mL in spiked urine gave false-positive PCP results on the Beckman Synchron assay; lamotrigine was reported with Bio-Rad TOX/See in a case report.

LSD screens cross-react with many drugs, most notably on the EMIT II LSD assay (amitriptyline, benzphetamine, bupropion, buspirone, cephradine, chlorpromazine, desipramine, diltiazem, doxepin, fentanyl, fluoxetine, haloperidol, imipramine, labetalol, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, risperidone, sertraline, thioridazine, trazodone and verapamil; also ergonovine, lysergol, brompheniramine, imipramine and methylphenidate at 4,000-50,000 ng/mL); the mucolytic ambroxol caused unexpected LSD positives in 12 patients (CEDIA DAU LSD); fentanyl (40 µg/L) and sertraline (1.5 µg/mL in spiked urine) triggered CEDIA LSD assays.

reporting_issues.issue: Table I labels the m-CPP entry of Baron et al. 'Native matrix' with a 300 µg/L cutoff, while the text describes dilution experiments of standards in water with a 1.0 µg/mL d-methamphetamine cutoff calibrator.
reporting_issues.consequence: The level of evidence and the cutoff for this entry are uncertain; check the primary paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Table III labels the efavirenz entry 'Retrospective chart review', while the text describes a blinded comparison of 50 patients taking efavirenz with 50 not taking it, plus spiking experiments.
reporting_issues.consequence: The table understates the evidence for efavirenz; use the text's description.

reporting_issues.issue: This review reports the Drug Screen Multi 5 test as negative on the efavirenz presumptive positives in Blank et al. (2009), while Moeller et al. (2017, PDF p. 12) say efavirenz interference with benzodiazepine screens occurs only with the Triage 8 and Drug Screen Multi 5 tests, citing the same study and Röder et al. (2007).
reporting_issues.consequence: Which point-of-care benzodiazepine tests react to efavirenz cannot be settled from the two reviews; read the primary papers before naming tests.

reporting_issues.issue: The method limits the search to articles after 2000 and says older ones only clarify (p. 1), but the tables include older reports as entries without marking them (for example ibuprofen and naproxen, 1990; ofloxacin on EMIT II opiates, 1997; the EMIT II LSD panel, 1997; ambroxol, 1998; verapamil and rifampicin, 1998), and the reference list of 62 entries, the same number as the included articles, also holds background papers (on amphetamine euphoria, opioid receptors and buprenorphine practice) and earlier reviews.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 62 included articles cannot be identified, and some listed interferences were found with assays that may no longer be in use.

reporting_issues.issue: The introduction states that in the majority of cases the cause of a false-positive screening result is unknown, without data or citation.
reporting_issues.consequence: It cannot be cited as a measured proportion.

reporting_issues.issue: The buprenorphine-assay cross-reactivity concentrations for morphine, methadone, codeine, dihydrocodeine and morphine-3-glucuronide are printed in mg/mL in the text and mg/L in Table V (consistent with each other), while most other entries use µg/mL or µg/L; units vary from row to row across the tables.
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers must convert before comparing with cutoffs in ng/mL; the buprenorphine figures were not checked against the primary paper (Pavlic et al., 2005) and should be before they are cited.

verification.source_read: PDF (Advance Access version, J Anal Toxicol, published online 1 July 2014, pages 1-10, which differ from the version of record, 38(7):387-396), all pages; Tables I-VI and Figures 1-2 checked on rendered pages, and units checked at 300 dpi because the text layer drops the micro sign; no supplement
